lessons.title: Body parts and what hurts: Mein Kopf tut weh
lessons.goal: Name ten body parts and say what hurts, with tut weh and -schmerzen.

grammar.point: Body parts are nouns with gender and plural; say what hurts with mein + body part + tut weh (plural: tun weh) or Ich habe + body part + Schmerzen.
grammar.oneLine: Mein Kopf tut weh. Meine Füße tun weh. Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.

mistake.why: Many things hurt, so the verb is tun, not tut.

terms.meaning: more than one: die Beine
a long word built from small words: Kopf + Schmerzen
hurts: tut for one thing, tun for many

cards.title: Before we start: what hurts
cards.body: Chapter 8 is about your body and health: what hurts, illness, the doctor, and giving advice with commands. Today you say your head hurts. You already know mein and the verb in second place.
steps: You already know: Das ist mein Bruder: mein + noun (chapter 5)
New today: mein + body part + tut weh says what hurts; for many parts, tun weh
By the end you can: name ten body parts and say what hurts

examples.why: New today: tut weh says it hurts.
New today: more than one part: tun weh.

cards.more: Your body is like a house with many rooms, and each room has its own word with der, die or das. To say a room hurts, German does not say I have pain. It says: my head does hurt. The small verb tut weh stays together like a pair of shoes: tut is in second place, weh goes to the end. If two parts hurt, tut becomes tun. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Body parts: der, die or das?
cards.body: Body parts are nouns, so each one has a gender and a plural. Learn the article with the word. Many plurals add an umlaut: der Kopf → die Köpfe, die Hand → die Hände, der Fuß → die Füße. Learn the plural too.
cards.more: Think of your body as a list of nouns. Each one wears a little tag: der, die or das. You can't see the tag, so you must learn it with the word. Step 1: say the word with its article: der Kopf. Step 2: say the plural: die Köpfe. Step 3: say it three times. Extra example: der Arm, die Arme = the arm, the arms.
cards.lead: The intro showed the plan for this lesson. On this card: body parts with der, die or das, so you can name the part of you that hurts.

deeper.text: Many body parts come in pairs: Auge, Ohr, Bein, Arm, Hand, Fuß. When you talk about both, German uses the plural, just as English says my eyes, not my eye. Learn each word with its plural from the start, because the plural is the form you will say most often.

cards.title: Mein Kopf tut weh
cards.body: To say that a body part hurts, use mein + body part + tut weh. tut weh means hurts. The little word weh goes to the very end, like the second verb in a sentence with a modal. Feminine words take meine: meine Hand.

examples.why: One thing hurts: tut. weh is last.

cards.more: Imagine you tell a friend: my head, it hurts. The German chunk for hurts is tut weh. Think of it like a separable verb: tut is in part 2 and weh waits at the end. Step 1: say mein or meine. Step 2: say the body part. Step 3: tut weh. Extra example: Mein Ohr tut weh. = My ear hurts.
cards.lead: You can name body parts with their articles. Next: the phrase for saying a body part hurts, so you can tell a doctor where it is.

deeper.text: Notice who does the hurting. In English you say I have a pain in my head. In German the body part itself is the subject: Mein Hals tut weh. The head hurts, and there is no ich in the sentence at all. That is why mein comes first and the verb right after the body part.

cards.title: More than one hurts: tun weh
cards.body: If two or more things hurt, tut becomes tun. The body part is plural, so use meine for all plural words. Meine Beine tun weh. Meine Füße tun weh. The plural of the verb ends in -n, like wir and sie (they) in chapter 2.
cards.more: Think of English: my foot hurts, but my feet hurt. English also changes the verb, from hurts to hurt. German does the same with tut and tun. The trick is to look at the noun first. Does it show more than one, with an ending like -e or -en, or an umlaut? Füße, Beine, Augen and Ohren all do. Then the verb takes -n: tun. Step 1: find the noun. Step 2: one or many? Step 3: tut or tun, and weh at the end. Extra example: Meine Ohren tun weh. = My ears hurt.
cards.lead: You can say one body part hurts. Next: what changes when two or more things hurt, so you can say your legs or your feet hurt.

deeper.text: One surprise: alles (everything) counts as one thing, even though it means many body parts. So you say Alles tut weh, with tut, not tun. You hear this after a long day or with the flu. The same goes for das: Das tut weh! (That hurts!) is what people shout when they bump into something. Both words take the singular verb.

cards.title: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen
cards.body: A second way to say it: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Schmerzen means pains. Put the body part in front: Kopf + Schmerzen = Kopfschmerzen. It is one long word, with no article. Compare: Mein Kopf tut weh = Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.
cards.more: Imagine a form at the doctor's. There is no space for a long sentence, so one word must do the job: Kopfschmerzen. That is why German loves glued words. English has a few too: headache, toothache, backache. German simply uses Schmerzen for all of them and puts the body part in front. Step 1: name the body part. Step 2: glue Schmerzen onto it. Step 3: put it after ich habe or er hat, with no ein. Extra example: Leon hat Rückenschmerzen. = Leon has back pain.
cards.lead: You can say a body part hurts. Next: a second way to say it, with the word Schmerzen, so you can say you have a headache or a stomach ache.

deeper.text: Kopfschmerzen is a plural word, so German uses no article: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen, not a headache. English says a headache, but German treats the pains as a group. The same goes for all words ending in -schmerzen. Just say haben + the word, nothing else.

cards.title: Ask and answer: Wo tut es weh?
cards.body: A doctor asks: Was ist los? (What is wrong?) and Wo tut es weh? (Where does it hurt?) You answer with a body part. Or you show the place and say Hier tut es weh. Here, es means it. The verb is still in part 2.

examples.why: Place first: verb is still part 2.

steps: The doctor asks: Wo tut es weh?
You say the place: Mein Bauch tut weh.
Or you point: Hier tut es weh.
cards.more: A doctor visit is a little game of questions and answers. The doctor asks, you answer. Step 1: listen for Wo? That means where. Step 2: answer with mein + body part + tut weh. Step 3: or point and say Hier. The doctor can also ask Was ist los? That means what is wrong? You can answer Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Extra example: Was ist los? Mein Fuß tut weh. = What is wrong? My foot hurts.
cards.lead: You have two ways to say what hurts. Next: the doctor's question Wo tut es weh? and how to answer it, so you can show where it hurts.

deeper.text: A place word can start the sentence. Hier tut es weh puts hier on chair 1, then the verb on chair 2, then es on chair 3. The rule you know from chapter 2 still applies. es is a little filler subject that means it. Da means there, so Da tut es weh points to another spot.

cards.title: Guess a new word from its parts
cards.body: German words are often built from words you already know. Look for the pieces. Kopfschmerzen = Kopf + Schmerzen. Handtasche = Hand + Tasche (a bag you carry in your hand). Fußball = Fuß + Ball. The last piece gives the gender: die Tasche → die Handtasche.

examples.why: Hand + Tasche; die Tasche → die Handtasche.

steps: Look for words you know inside the long word.
Read the pieces from left to right.
The last piece says what it is and gives the gender.
cards.more: A long German word looks scary, but it is a train of small words. Step 1: find the cars. Handtasche has two: Hand and Tasche. Step 2: guess the meaning: hand bag. Step 3: the last car is the boss. Tasche is feminine, so die Handtasche. This trick helps you read signs and doctor words. Extra example: Halsschmerzen = Hals + Schmerzen = neck pain, a sore throat.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: guessing new long words from their parts, so you can work out a word like Handtasche without a dictionary.

deeper.text: Sometimes a little glue sound sits between the pieces of a long word, like the -en in Ohrenschmerzen. You do not need a rule for this. Just learn those words as they come. The last piece still gives the gender, so die Handtasche is feminine because die Tasche is.

Look at the body-part table: a die-word.

lessons.title: Illness and symptoms: Ich habe Fieber
lessons.goal: Say what illness or symptom you have, say you do not have one, and say since when.

grammar.point: Say an illness with haben (Ich habe Fieber; eine Erkältung), say what you do not have with kein/keinen/keine, and say since when with seit + a time word.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe seit gestern Fieber. Ich habe keinen Husten.

mistake.why: Fieber is a das-word, so it takes kein. Only masculine words take keinen.

terms.meaning: a sign of an illness: Fieber, Husten
since: seit gestern = since yesterday
no: kein for das-words, keinen for masculine objects, keine for die-words and plurals

cards.title: Before we start: I am ill
cards.body: You are at the doctor and she asks what is wrong. You say: I have a fever. The verb haben does the job, the one you know from chapter 2. A new little word, seit, tells since when.
steps: You already know: Ich habe Hunger: haben + a thing (chapter 2), and keinen (chapter 4)
New today: haben + illness, kein for none, and seit + a time word for since when
By the end you can: say what illness you have, that you do not have one, and since when

examples.why: You know this already: haben + a thing.

examples.en: I have had a fever since yesterday.
examples.why: New today: seit gestern says since when.

cards.more: Germans do not say I am a fever. They say I have a fever, like I have hunger. So the verb haben, which you already know, does all the work. To say you do not have it, you use kein, keinen or keine, the same as with food in chapter 4. The new helper is seit: it points back to the moment it started. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Illness words: Ich habe Fieber
cards.body: To name an illness, use haben: Ich habe Fieber. Fieber, Husten, Schnupfen and Grippe usually take no ein. Erkältung is feminine and countable, so you say eine Erkältung. Learn the article with each word.
cards.more: Picture a doctor's waiting room. Each person carries an invisible bag with an illness in it: Fieber, Husten, Schnupfen. They all say Ich habe and then the illness, right after the verb. English often needs a: a cough, a fever. German leaves the little word out for most illnesses. The article only matters again when you say no, with kein or keinen. Only die Erkältung behaves like a countable thing and needs eine. Extra example: Mira hat Schnupfen. = Mira has a runny nose.
cards.lead: You can name body parts and say what hurts. Next: illness words and the verb haben, so you can say you have a fever or a cough.

deeper.text: Illness names without an article are common in English too: I have flu, I have fever. German does the same for Fieber, Husten and Grippe. Erkältung is different: it is a countable word, like a cold, so you need eine. Learn which kind each word is when you meet it.

cards.title: I have no fever: kein, keine
cards.body: To say you do not have something, use kein, as in chapters 3 and 4. Fieber is neuter: kein Fieber. Husten and Schnupfen are masculine and the object, so they take keinen. die-words take keine: keine Erkältung, keine Schmerzen.
cards.more: Think of kein as ein with a no sign in front. Wherever ein would stand, kein stands, and it takes the same ending. Ich habe einen Termin, ich habe keinen Husten: the -en is the same in both. That is why you must know the gender of every illness word. A good trick: say the pair aloud, der Husten, keinen Husten, until it sounds right. Step 1: which gender? Step 2: is it the object? Step 3: pick kein, keinen or keine. Extra example: Er hat keinen Schnupfen. = He has no runny nose.
cards.lead: You can say you have a fever or a cough. Next: kein with illness words, so you can say you have no fever or no cough.

deeper.text: kein negates a noun, but it does not negate an adjective. For krank, müde and similar words, use nicht: Ich bin nicht krank, never kein krank. A good rule: no thing, use kein. Not an action or a quality, use nicht. This works for the whole chapter.

cards.title: How do you feel? Ich bin krank
cards.body: Wie geht's? is a greeting. You can answer: Gut, or Nicht so gut, or Schlecht. To say you are ill, use sein: Ich bin krank. Ich bin müde. The adjective has no ending after sein.
cards.more: Sein works like an equals sign: I = ill. Step 1: choose sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist. Step 2: add the adjective. Nothing changes at the end of the adjective. You can also say how bad it is: sehr krank. Extra example: Wie geht's? Nicht so gut. Ich bin krank. = How are you? Not so good. I am ill.
cards.lead: You can name illnesses. Next: how to say how you feel with sein, so you can say you are ill or tired and answer How are you?

deeper.text: Wie geht's? is short for Wie geht es dir? The apostrophe replaces the e of es. The usual reply is Gut, danke, und dir? which means fine, thanks, and you? Germans often answer more honestly than English speakers, so Nicht so gut is a normal answer, not rude.

cards.title: Since when? Seit wann? Seit gestern
cards.body: A doctor asks: Seit wann haben Sie Fieber? Seit wann means since when. Answer with seit + time: seit gestern (since yesterday), seit heute, seit Montag. Learn each as one piece. The verb stays in part 2.

examples.en: Since when do you have a fever?
I have had a fever since yesterday.
I have had a cough since Monday.
examples.why: Time first: verb is still part 2.

cards.more: In English you say I have had a cough since Monday. In German you just say I have a cough since Monday. Same verb, haben. Step 1: ask Seit wann? Step 2: answer seit + a time word you know. Step 3: keep the verb in part 2. Extra example: Seit heute habe ich Bauchschmerzen. = Since today I have a stomach ache.
cards.lead: You can say how you feel. Next: the doctor's question Seit wann?, so you can say how long you have had a problem.

deeper.text: German uses the present tense where English uses have had. Ich habe seit gestern Fieber is literally I have fever since yesterday. You do not need a past tense for something that is still going on. This is easier than English: one tense, and seit does the work.

example.en: Ben has been ill since Monday.

cards.title: Going to the doctor
cards.body: To say you go to the doctor, learn: Ich gehe zum Arzt. A woman doctor is die Ärztin: zur Ärztin. To get an appointment, use a chunk you know: Ich möchte einen Termin, bitte. Why zum and zur: chapter 7.

examples.en: I am going to the doctor.
I must go to the doctor (female).
examples.why: Chunk: zur Ärztin. muss + gehen last.

examples.en: I would like an appointment, please.

cards.more: Learn zum Arzt as a block, the way you learned mit dem Bus. Do not take it apart yet. A man doctor: zum Arzt. A woman doctor: zur Ärztin. You know the reason from chapter 7. For an appointment you ask politely with möchte. Step 1: Ich möchte einen Termin. Step 2: add bitte. Extra example: Ich gehe zum Arzt. = I go to the doctor.
cards.lead: You learned zum and zur in chapter 7. Next: going to the doctor and asking for an appointment, so you can say where you are going and why.

deeper.text: This connects to chapter 7: zu is going, bei is being there. So you go zum Arzt, but you have an appointment beim Arzt, because the appointment is with the doctor. A woman doctor needs bei der Ärztin. Notice the umlaut: Arzt becomes Ärztin, and the plural is Ärzte.

example.de: Ich habe einen Termin beim Arzt.
example.en: I have an appointment at the doctor's.

cards.title: At the doctor: put it all together
cards.body: A short doctor talk has four steps. The doctor asks Was haben Sie? You say what you have. The doctor asks Wo tut es weh? You show the place. The doctor asks Seit wann? You say seit gestern or seit Montag. New: der Zahn (tooth), die Zähne.

examples.en: I have had a toothache since yesterday.

steps: Doctor: Was haben Sie?
You: Ich habe Fieber. Mein Kopf tut weh.
Doctor: Seit wann?
You: Seit gestern.
cards.more: A doctor visit follows the same path every time, like a little map. Step 1: the doctor asks what is wrong: Was haben Sie? Step 2: you answer with haben and an illness, or with mein + body part + tut weh. Step 3: the doctor asks Seit wann? Step 4: you say seit + time. If you learn these four lines, you can survive a visit. Extra example: Ich habe seit Montag Fieber. = I have had a fever since Monday.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: the four steps of a doctor talk, so you can say what is wrong, where it hurts and since when, in one visit.

deeper.text: At the doctor's you do not need whole sentences. Fieber. Seit gestern. is understood perfectly. But a short full sentence is also easy: Mein Kopf tut seit gestern weh. Notice that seit gestern sits in the middle, and weh stays at the very end of the sentence.

example.de: Mein Kopf tut seit gestern weh.
example.en: My head has hurt since yesterday.

lessons.title: Age, height and weight: Wie alt, wie groß?
lessons.goal: Give and ask age, height and weight, and decline a personal question politely.

grammar.point: Ask Wie alt / Wie groß / Wie viel wiegst du? and answer with sein (alt, groß) or wiegen; refuse politely with Das ist privat or Das möchte ich nicht sagen.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bin 25 Jahre alt. Ich wiege 70 Kilo. Das möchte ich nicht sagen.

mistake.why: German uses sein for age, not haben.

terms.meaning: to weigh: ich wiege, du wiegst, er wiegt
to say no politely
a question about private things, like age or weight

cards.title: Before we start: age, height and weight
cards.body: At the doctor, the form asks how old you are, how tall and how heavy. You already know Wie alt bist du? Today you add two more questions and a polite way to say no.
steps: You already know: Wie alt bist du? (chapter 2)
New today: Wie groß ...? and Wie viel wiegst du? with sein and wiegen
By the end you can: say your age, height and weight, and refuse a personal question politely

examples.why: New today: the same pattern with groß.
New today: wiegen is a new verb for weight.

cards.more: You already own a tool for asking about a person: wie plus a describing word plus bist plus du. Wie alt asks for age, wie groß asks for height. For weight you use a new verb, wiegen, and it works like all your other verbs. If someone asks something too personal, you do not have to answer. German has polite ways to say it. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: How old are you? Wie alt?
cards.body: You know numbers up to 100 from chapter 2. To ask the age: Wie alt bist du? (friend) or Wie alt sind Sie? (polite). Answer: Ich bin 25 Jahre alt, or just Ich bin 25. Note: German says I am 25 years old.
cards.more: Picture a birthday cake with candles. German counts the candles with sein: Ich bin 25. English does the same with be: I am 25. Some languages say I have 25 years, but German never uses haben here. The long form adds Jahre alt at the end. Numbers over 20 come backwards: fünfundzwanzig is five and twenty. Step 1: Wie alt? Step 2: bin, bist, ist or sind. Step 3: the number, and Jahre alt if you like. Extra example: Anna ist 26 Jahre alt. = Anna is 26 years old.
cards.lead: The doctor asked what is wrong. Next: the doctor's other questions, starting with age, so you can ask and answer how old someone is.

deeper.text: Careful with the short answer. You can say Ich bin 25 or Ich bin 25 Jahre alt, but not Ich bin 25 Jahre: alt must come with Jahre. For one year, use the singular: ein Jahr alt. From two on, it is Jahre. So a small child is ein Jahr alt, and a big sister is zehn Jahre alt.

example.de: Das Kind ist ein Jahr alt.
example.en: The child is one year old.

cards.title: How tall are you? Wie groß?
cards.body: To ask the height: Wie groß bist du? groß means big, and for people tall. Say the height with Meter and the centimetres (der Zentimeter): 1,75 m = ein Meter fünfundsiebzig. Then add groß: Ich bin ein Meter fünfundsiebzig groß.

examples.de: Ich bin ein Meter siebzig groß.
Mira ist ein Meter fünfundsechzig groß.
examples.why: The centimetres are a number: fünfundsechzig.

cards.more: Picture a measuring tape on the wall of the doctor's office. You read two numbers: the metre and the centimetres. German says them one after the other: ein Meter, fünfundsiebzig. English says one seventy-five, almost the same. Some people give only the centimetres: Ich bin 175 Zentimeter groß. Both are fine. Step 1: ein Meter. Step 2: the centimetres as one number. Step 3: groß at the end. Extra example: Ben ist ein Meter achtzig groß. = Ben is 1.80 m tall.
cards.lead: You can answer questions about age. Next: height, with metres and centimetres, so you can say how tall you are.

deeper.text: Look at how the height is written: 1,75 m. German uses a comma where English uses a point, so 1,75 is one point seven five. You see the same on prices: 2,50 Euro. When you write your height on a German form, use the comma. When you say it, the comma disappears: ein Meter fünfundsiebzig.

cards.title: How much do you weigh? wiegen
cards.body: To ask the weight: Wie viel wiegst du? The verb is wiegen (to weigh). It is regular: ich wiege, du wiegst, er/sie wiegt, wir wiegen, Sie wiegen. Say the number and Kilo, with no plural: 70 Kilo. schwer means heavy.
cards.more: Think of a bathroom scale. You step on it and read the number. Then you say Ich wiege, the number and Kilo. wiegen is a normal verb, so it follows the pattern of wohnen or kommen: ich wiege, du wiegst, er wiegt. English says kilos with an s, but after a number German keeps Kilo with no ending. If a thing weighs a lot, it is schwer: Die Tasche ist schwer. Step 1: Ich wiege. Step 2: the number. Step 3: Kilo. Extra example: Mira wiegt 55 Kilo. = Mira weighs 55 kilos.
cards.lead: You can say your height. Next: weight and the verb wiegen, so you can answer how much you weigh.

deeper.text: Units stay singular after a number: 70 Kilo, zwei Meter. English adds an s to kilos and metres, German does not. The verb wiegen is regular, with one small point: the stem ends in g, so du wiegst takes just -st, with no extra e. Easy to say, easy to write.

cards.title: Polite questions at the doctor: Sie
cards.body: A doctor says Sie to adults. The three questions for Sie are Wie alt sind Sie? Wie groß sind Sie? Wie viel wiegen Sie? Only the verb form and the person change. Compare with du: bist and wiegst become sind and wiegen.
cards.more: Picture two doors at the doctor's: one for friends and one for adults you do not know well. Behind the friend door you hear bist and wiegst. Behind the adult door you hear sind and wiegen. The question word stays the same, only the verb changes. Sie takes the same verb form as sie (they): Sie sind, sie sind; Sie wiegen, sie wiegen. Only the capital S tells them apart in writing. Step 1: du or Sie? Step 2: pick the verb. Extra example: Wie alt sind Sie? = How old are you? (polite)
cards.lead: You can ask these questions with du. Next: the polite Sie form of the same questions, so you can ask an adult at the doctor's.

deeper.text: With Sie, the verb always looks like the infinitive: wiegen Sie, haben Sie, kommen Sie. The only exception is sein, which becomes sind. So if you know the infinitive, you know the polite form already. This makes formal speech easier than it sounds.

example.en: How much time do you have?

cards.title: A personal question? Say no politely
cards.body: In Germany, weight and age can feel private. Some questions (die Frage, die Fragen) are zu persönlich (too personal). Refuse politely: Das ist privat. or Das möchte ich nicht sagen. The second one is a modal sentence: möchte is part 2 and sagen goes to the end.

examples.en: I would rather not say that.
Sorry, I do not say that.

steps: Smile.
Say Entschuldigung.
Say Das ist privat. or Das möchte ich nicht sagen.
cards.more: You do not have to answer every question. A short, friendly refusal is normal. Step 1: smile. Step 2: say Entschuldigung (sorry). Step 3: say your refusal. In Das möchte ich nicht sagen, the word Das comes first, but the verb is still in part 2. The pronoun ich goes after it. Extra example: Das sage ich nicht. = I am not saying that.
cards.lead: You can ask for age, height and weight. Next: how to say no politely to a personal question, so you can refuse without being rude.

deeper.text: In a refusal like Das möchte ich nicht sagen, nicht sits in front of the last verb. The modal is at chair 2, and the infinitive with nicht closes the sentence. You can add a time word before nicht: heute nicht sagen. The pattern stays, and it works with every modal.

steps: Doctor: Wie alt sind Sie?

cards.more: Think of the form as three small boxes: age, height, weight. For each box you can fill it in or politely skip it. Step 1: listen for alt, groß or wie viel. Step 2: answer with the right pattern: bin … alt, bin … groß, wiege … Kilo. Step 3: or refuse with Das ist privat. Extra example: Ich wiege 60 Kilo. = I weigh 60 kilos.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: a doctor's form in one go, so you can answer the questions about age and height, and decline the one about weight.

deeper.text: Forms use nouns built from the words you know. alt gives das Alter (age), groß gives die Größe (height), and wiegen goes with das Gewicht (weight). Spotting the connection helps you learn new words faster. You will meet these nouns on a form, but when you speak, you use the adjective: Wie groß bist du?

lessons.title: Commands for Sie: Nehmen Sie eine Tablette!
lessons.goal: Give polite instructions with Sie: regular, sein, separable and negative, and talk about medicine.

grammar.point: The Sie command is verb first + Sie (no stem change): Nehmen Sie! sein is Seien Sie!; a separable verb sends its prefix to the end: Rufen Sie an!; no uses nicht or kein.
grammar.oneLine: Nehmen Sie dreimal am Tag eine Tablette. Seien Sie pünktlich. Rufen Sie an.

mistake.why: The stem change (nimmt) is only for du and er. For Sie the command uses the infinitive.

terms.meaning: a command: it tells someone to do something
the small first part of a separable verb: an in anrufen
a prescription from the doctor

cards.title: Before we start: polite commands at the doctor
cards.body: At the doctor and the pharmacy, people tell you what to do: Take a tablet, wait please. You already know the polite command from chapter 3, when you asked for the way. Today it moves to health.
steps: You already know: Gehen Sie geradeaus! the Sie command (chapter 3)
New today: the Sie command for health: Nehmen Sie, Seien Sie, Rufen Sie an
By the end you can: give and understand polite instructions with Sie

examples.why: You know this already. Verb first, then Sie.
New today: the same shape with nehmen and a tablet.
New today: sein is irregular, so the command is Seien Sie.

cards.more: The polite command is a pattern you already have in your toolbox: the verb stands at the front, then Sie. Gehen Sie, Nehmen Sie. Nothing new to build, only new things to say. A few verbs are special: sein becomes Seien Sie, and a separable verb sends its small piece to the end, like Rufen Sie an. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: The Sie command: a quick refresher
cards.body: A command (imperative) tells someone to do something. You know the polite command from chapter 3: the verb comes first, then Sie. Gehen Sie geradeaus! The verb has the same form as the infinitive. Add bitte to be friendly.

examples.why: im Bett: in + dem = im, like im Kino (chapter 7).

cards.more: Think of a waiter or a doctor speaking to you: they always use this shape. It looks like a yes/no question, only your voice goes down at the end instead of up. Trinken Sie Tee? asks. Trinken Sie Tee! tells. English simply drops you: Drink tea! German keeps Sie, because the polite form needs it. Step 1: the infinitive first. Step 2: Sie. Step 3: the rest, and bitte if you like. Extra example: Kommen Sie bitte. = Please come.
cards.lead: You can ask a doctor's questions. Next: a command for an adult with Sie, so you can tell a patient what to do, like take a tablet.

deeper.text: A Sie command looks just like a yes/no question: Gehen Sie? and Gehen Sie! share the same word order. The difference is in your voice and in the mark at the end. A command falls at the end and has a full stop or exclamation mark. A question rises and has a question mark.

cards.title: Stem-changing verbs: nothing changes for Sie
cards.body: Verbs like nehmen, essen, lesen and fahren change their stem for du and er (du nimmst). Not for Sie. The Sie command always uses the infinitive: Nehmen Sie! Essen Sie! Lesen Sie! Fahren Sie!
cards.more: Imagine a verb with two faces. With du and er it wears a costume: nimmst, nimmt, isst, liest, fährt. With Sie it takes the costume off and shows its plain face, the infinitive. The Sie command always uses that plain face. So you never have to remember Nimmen or Fähren, because they do not exist. Step 1: think of the infinitive. Step 2: put it first. Step 3: add Sie. Extra example: Fahren Sie langsam. = Drive slowly.
cards.lead: You know the Sie command. Next: verbs that change their stem for du, and why the Sie command does not change, so you can tell a patient to take or eat something.

deeper.text: On signs, forms and medicine boxes, German often drops Sie and uses only the infinitive: Bitte warten. Nicht rauchen. This sounds short and neutral, not rude, because it speaks to everyone. When you talk to a person, use the full command with Sie. When you read a box or a sign, expect the infinitive.

cards.title: sein: Seien Sie ruhig!
cards.body: The verb sein is irregular again. The Sie command is not Sind Sie! but Seien Sie! Learn it as a block: Seien Sie bitte ruhig. Seien Sie pünktlich. Use it with an adjective, like ruhig or pünktlich.
cards.more: Most verbs are easy: infinitive plus Sie. Sein is the odd one. It has its own command word, seien. Step 1: do not say sind. Step 2: say seien. Step 3: add Sie and an adjective. Extra example: Seien Sie bitte pünktlich. = Please be on time. Learn all three together: Seien Sie, sei, seid. You will see sei and seid soon.
cards.lead: You can give Sie commands with normal verbs. Next: the irregular Sie command of sein, so you can say be calm or be on time.

deeper.text: Compare a question and a command. Sind Sie ruhig? asks whether you are calm. Seien Sie ruhig! tells you to be calm. The command uses a different form of sein, which looks odd, so learn Seien Sie as one block, the way you learn a short phrase.

cards.title: Separable verbs: Rufen Sie an!
cards.body: A separable verb splits in a command. The main verb is first, then Sie, and the prefix goes to the very end. anrufen → Rufen Sie an! aufstehen → Stehen Sie auf! It works like a normal sentence with Sie.

examples.why: Verb first; the prefix an is last.
Verb first; the prefix auf is last.

examples.de: Rufen Sie bitte Frau Weber an.
examples.why: The prefix an waits at the end.

cards.more: Picture a sandwich. The top slice is the verb: Rufen. The bottom slice is the prefix: an. Everything else is the filling: Sie, mich, bitte, morgen. English keeps get up together, but German puts the filling in between. The prefix carries the meaning, so never forget it: without auf, Stehen Sie! just means stand. Step 1: split the verb. Step 2: verb, Sie, filling. Step 3: the prefix last. Extra example: Kommen Sie bitte mit. = Please come along.
cards.lead: You can give a command with sein. Next: separable verbs in a Sie command, so you can say call me or get up slowly.

deeper.text: A separable verb works like a frame: the verb comes first, the prefix goes to the very end, and everything else sits in between. Objects, bitte and time words all go inside the frame. The longer the sentence, the further apart the two halves are.

cards.title: Medicine forms and how often
cards.body: Learn three medicine forms: die Tablette, der Tropfen (plural die Tropfen), die Salbe. To say how often, use einmal, zweimal, dreimal + am Tag (a day). Nehmen Sie dreimal am Tag eine Tablette. Learn am Tag as one chunk.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie dreimal am Tag eine Tablette.
examples.en: Take one tablet three times a day.
examples.why: dreimal am Tag = three times a day.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie zweimal am Tag zehn Tropfen.
examples.en: Take ten drops twice a day.
Take the tablet in the evening.

cards.more: Read a German medicine box like a short recipe. It answers two questions: how much and how often. How much: eine Tablette, zehn Tropfen. How often: einmal, zweimal or dreimal am Tag. The doctor usually says how often first, then how much: Nehmen Sie zweimal am Tag zehn Tropfen. A tip: Tropfen looks the same in the singular and the plural, so the number tells you. Extra example: Nehmen Sie einmal am Tag eine Tablette. = Take one tablet once a day.
cards.lead: You can tell a patient what to do. Next: medicine words and how often to take them, so you can read a dose on a medicine box.

deeper.text: The ending -mal means times. Put it after a number: einmal, zweimal, dreimal, viermal. You can use it with any number, so viermal is four times and fünfmal is five times. The word Tag stays the same, so you only need to change the number.

example.de: Nehmen Sie viermal am Tag eine Tablette.
example.en: Take a tablet four times a day.

cards.title: Do not! nicht and kein
cards.body: To say do not, use nicht or kein, as in a normal sentence. nicht usually goes at the end: Arbeiten Sie nicht. kein replaces ein or no article: Trinken Sie keinen Kaffee. Masculine objects take keinen.

examples.de: Gehen Sie heute nicht zur Arbeit.
examples.en: Do not go to work today.

cards.more: A no-command is a command with a no word. Step 1: do you say no to an action? Use nicht: Arbeiten Sie nicht. Step 2: do you say no to a thing? Use kein: keinen Kaffee, keine Tabletten. Masculine things change to keinen, as you learned for the object. Extra example: Essen Sie keine Wurst. = Do not eat sausage.
cards.lead: You can say what to take. Next: saying do not with nicht and kein, so you can warn someone what to avoid.

deeper.text: In a command, nicht usually stands near the end. It comes before a place or direction chunk like zum Arzt or zur Arbeit, and before the verb prefix if there is one: Gehen Sie nicht zum Arzt. Arbeiten Sie nicht. Stehen Sie nicht auf. A time word like heute comes before nicht: Gehen Sie heute nicht zur Arbeit.

Step 3: the pharmacist tells you what to do, with commands like Nehmen Sie … Step 4: you say Danke and hear Gute Besserung! The chunks mit dem Rezept and zur Apotheke you learn as whole pieces. Extra example: Ich brauche ein Medikament. = I need a medicine.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: a visit to the pharmacy, so you can ask for your medicine and understand what the pharmacist says back.

deeper.text: You say Gute Besserung! to anyone who is ill, not only at the pharmacy. Besserung means getting better, so the wish is good improvement. It is polite and friendly, and you can say it to a colleague, a friend or a neighbour. People also write it in messages.

lessons.title: Commands for du: Nimm! Fahr! Sei!
lessons.goal: Give instructions to a friend with the du command, including stem changes, sein and separable verbs.

grammar.point: The du command is the du form without du and -st (Komm! Trink!); e → i stays (Nimm! Iss! Lies!), a → ä does not (Fahr! Schlaf!), sein is Sei!, and a separable verb sends its prefix to the end (Ruf an!).
grammar.oneLine: Komm! Nimm eine Tablette! Fahr langsam! Sei pünktlich! Ruf mich an!

mistake.why: The change e → i stays in the du command: du nimmst → Nimm.

terms.meaning: the command for one friend: Komm!
a vowel change in du and er/sie: nehmen → nimmt
the small first part of a separable verb: an in anrufen

cards.title: Before we start: commands for a friend
cards.body: Your friend Leon is ill. You do not say Sie to a friend, you say du. Today you give friendly advice: Nimm eine Tablette. You already know the polite command and the du forms of verbs.
steps: You already know: Nehmen Sie eine Tablette (last lesson) and du nimmst, du fährst (chapters 2 and 6)
New today: the du command: take the du form, drop du and -st
By the end you can: give friendly instructions with du, like Nimm! Fahr langsam! Sei pünktlich!

examples.why: You know this already. The Sie command from the last lesson.
New today: the du command is shorter: Nimm, with no du.
New today: the ä of du fährst goes away in the command: Fahr.

cards.more: With a friend, the command gets shorter, like a text message. You take your du form, for example du nimmst, and throw away the du and the ending: Nimm! The e to i change stays, so Nimm and Iss. But the a to ä change goes away: Fahr, not Fähr. Sein is odd: Sei. A separable verb sends its piece to the end, like Ruf an. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: The du command: take off -st
cards.body: To a friend you say du, and the command has no du in it. Recipe: take the du form and remove du and -st. du kommst → Komm! du trinkst → Trink! du gehst → Geh! One short word, often with bitte.
cards.more: Friends do not need long commands. Step 1: take the verb for du: du trinkst. Step 2: throw away du. Step 3: throw away -st. What is left is the command: Trink! Compare with Sie: Trinken Sie! (longer and more polite). Same idea, two sizes. Extra example: Warte hier. is for a friend, Warten Sie hier. is for a stranger.
cards.lead: You can give Sie commands to adults. Next: the du command for a friend, so you can tell someone close what to do.

deeper.text: The du command is almost the same as in English: the bare verb with nothing added. Come! is Komm!, and Drink! is Trink!. Add bitte to be friendly, and it is no longer blunt. With a friend, a short command is normal and warm, not rude.

cards.title: e → i stays: Nimm! Iss! Lies!
cards.body: Some verbs change e to i or ie for du (du nimmst, du isst, du liest). The command keeps this change. nehmen → Nimm! essen → Iss! lesen → Lies! sprechen → Sprich! sehen → Sieh! The Sie command does not change, but du does.
cards.more: Think of the du command as the du form with a haircut. du nimmst loses du and -st, and what is left is Nimm. The haircut does not change the colour: the i stays. So if you know du isst, you know the command for essen. If you know du liest, you know the one for lesen. English has nothing like this, so practise it aloud. Step 1: say the du form. Step 2: cut du and -st. Step 3: keep the vowel. Extra example: Sprich lauter! = Speak louder!
cards.lead: You can make du commands. Next: the vowel change in verbs like nehmen and essen, so you can say Take or Eat to a friend.

deeper.text: Stem-changing verbs never add an e in the command: it is Nimm!, not Nimme!, and Sprich!, not Spreche!. The command is short, just the stem. Also notice the spelling: nehmen becomes nimm with a double m. Say it, and the double m will feel natural.

cards.title: a → ä does NOT stay: Fahr! Schlaf!
cards.body: Careful: verbs with a → ä (du fährst, du schläfst) lose the umlaut in the command. fahren → Fahr! schlafen → Schlaf! Only e → i and e → ie stay. The a → ä change does not come along.

examples.why: mit dem Bus is a chunk.

cards.more: Imagine two teams of verbs. Team i (nehmen, essen, lesen, sprechen) keeps its new vowel in the command: Nimm, Iss, Lies, Sprich. Team ä (fahren, schlafen) leaves the umlaut at home: Fahr, Schlaf. A quick test for team ä: say the infinitive and cut -en. fahr-en gives Fahr, schlaf-en gives Schlaf. Step 1: which team is the verb in? Step 2: build the command. Step 3: add the rest. Extra example: Fahr bitte vorsichtig. = Please drive carefully.
cards.lead: You know the e to i change in du commands. Next: verbs with an umlaut that disappears in the command, so you can say Drive or Sleep correctly.

deeper.text: A way to remember it: the i stays, the umlaut goes. For nimmst and sprichst, the new vowel stays in the command. For fährst and schläfst, the ä goes back to a. You will hear Schlaf gut! all the time as a goodnight wish between friends.

cards.title: Extra e, and the odd one: sei
cards.body: Verbs with a stem ending in -t (warten, arbeiten) take an extra e: Warte! Arbeite! The verb sein is irregular again: du bist → Sei! Learn it by heart: Sei ruhig! Sei pünktlich! For Sie it is Seien Sie! die Ruhe = rest, quiet.
cards.more: Picture the word Wart! It ends hard, like a door that slams. German adds a soft -e to open it again: Warte! The same happens with arbeiten: Arbeite! You know this extra e from du wartest and du arbeitest. Then there is sein, the rebel of the verb family. It follows no pattern, so it has its own command: Sei! English uses be for everyone, German has Seien Sie, Sei and Seid. Step 1: stem ends in -t? Add -e. Step 2: sein? Say Sei. Extra example: Sei ruhig! = Be quiet!
cards.lead: You can handle the vowel changes. Next: verbs with a stem ending in t, and the odd form of sein, so you can say Wait or Be calm to a friend.

deeper.text: The extra e is also needed when the stem ends in -d: finden becomes Finde! With other verbs you may see an -e in old books or very careful writing, like Komme! or Gehe! In everyday German nobody says that. So stems in -t and -d need the -e, and all other verbs drop it.

cards.title: Separable verbs: Ruf an! Steh auf!
cards.body: A separable verb splits in a command: the verb goes first and the prefix goes to the end. anrufen → Ruf an! aufstehen → Steh auf! mitkommen → Komm mit! einkaufen → Kauf ein! It is the same as with Sie, but without Sie.
cards.more: Think of a sandwich again. The bread on top is the verb: Ruf. The bread at the bottom is the prefix: an. In between go the other words: mich, bitte, morgen. With a friend there is no Sie, so the sandwich is even thinner. A useful verb is mitnehmen: Nimm die Tasche mit! It shows two rules at once, e to i and the prefix at the end. Step 1: split the verb. Step 2: make the du command. Step 3: the prefix last. Extra example: Ruf mich morgen an. = Call me tomorrow.
cards.lead: You can say Be calm to a friend. Next: separable verbs in du commands, so you can say Call me or Get up to a friend.

deeper.text: The frame works the same way as with Sie. The verb goes first, the prefix goes last, and everything else sits in between. Short words like mich, bitte and a time such as um sieben fit inside. So the du command is a small frame with one short verb.

cards.title: At the doctor: commands for a friend
cards.body: A friend who plays doctor can say: Mach den Mund auf! (Open your mouth!) or Mach die Augen zu! (Close your eyes!) Both are separable: aufmachen, zumachen. Also zuhören: Hör zu! and aufpassen: Pass auf!
steps: Doctor: Mach den Mund auf.
Doctor: Mach die Augen zu.
Doctor: Pass auf!
Doctor: Fertig! (fertig = finished, done)
cards.more: Picture a children's doctor talking to a small boy. She does not say Sie, she says du: Mach den Mund auf! Mach die Augen zu! Hör gut zu! The tiny words auf and zu do the work. auf means open and zu means closed, so the same verb machen gets two opposite meanings. When she is done, she says: Fertig! Step 1: choose machen, hören or passen. Step 2: make the du command. Step 3: add the object. Step 4: auf or zu last. Extra example: Pass auf! = Watch out!
cards.lead: You can give du commands. Next: friendly doctor commands, so you can play doctor with a friend and say Open your mouth.

deeper.text: auf and zu are opposites, so the two separable verbs are a pair. aufmachen means open, and zumachen means close. You can use the pair with many things: the door, the window, your mouth. If you remember one, you remember the other.

cards.title: Friendly tips: do and do not
cards.body: A good tip is a short command. For no, use nicht or kein, as with Sie. Iss viel Gemüse. Mach Sport. Geh früh ins Bett. And: Arbeite nicht. Trink keinen Kaffee. Learn ins Bett as a chunk, like ins Kino.
steps: Say the tip as a command.
For no to an action: add nicht.
For no to a thing: use kein, keinen or keine.
cards.more: Tips from a friend are just short commands. Step 1: pick the verb and make the du command. Step 2: add your words. Step 3: do you want to say do not? For an action use nicht (Arbeite nicht). For a thing use kein (Trink keinen Kaffee). Masculine things change to keinen. Extra example: Iss keine Wurst. = Do not eat sausage.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: friendly tips with du, so you can give advice like Eat vegetables and also say what not to do.

deeper.text: Compare im Bett and ins Bett. You know this from chapter 7. Bleib im Bett means stay in bed, where you already are. Geh ins Bett means go to bed, with movement into it. The command verb tells you which one to use: bleiben stays, gehen moves.

cards.title: Before we start: commands for several friends
cards.body: Leon and Mira are both ill. You give advice to both at once. Which command do you use? You know ihr from chapter 2, so this fits right in. Then you learn to choose between Sie, du and ihr.
steps: You already know: Nimm eine Tablette (last lesson), and ihr nehmt, ihr seid (chapters 2 and 5)
New today: the ihr command: take the ihr form and drop ihr
By the end you can: give instructions to several friends, and choose between Sie, du and ihr

New today: sein is irregular, so the ihr command is Seid.

cards.more: Now you have three commands, like three keys on one key ring. Sie for strangers and polite talk, du for one friend, ihr for several friends. To make the ihr command you take the ihr form you already know, and you drop the word ihr. That is all. Then you practise choosing the right key by asking: who am I talking to? Step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: The ihr command: the ihr form without ihr
cards.body: To two or more friends (ihr) the command is the ihr form without ihr. ihr kommt → Kommt! ihr trinkt → Trinkt! ihr geht → Geht! It ends in -t. It looks like the statement, but the verb comes first and ihr is gone.
cards.more: Picture a teacher in front of a group. She does not say ihr, she just says Kommt! or Hört zu! The ending -t tells everyone that she means all of them. English has no special plural you, so it says Come! to one person or to ten. German shows the difference in the verb. Step 1: say the ihr form: ihr hört zu. Step 2: drop ihr. Step 3: verb first: Hört zu! Extra example: Trinkt viel Wasser. = Drink a lot of water (to several people).
cards.lead: You can give du commands to one friend. Next: the same kind of command to two or more friends, with ihr, so you can speak to a group.

deeper.text: Kommt! looks exactly like er kommt or ihr kommt. Only the position and the missing subject show that it is a command. In writing the exclamation mark helps, and in speech your voice falls. If you add ihr, it becomes a question: Kommt ihr mit? means are you coming along? So never put ihr into the command.

cards.title: Stem changers with ihr: no change
cards.body: For ihr, verbs do not change their stem, because ihr never does: ihr nehmt, ihr esst, ihr lest, ihr fahrt. So the command has no i and no umlaut: Nehmt! Esst! Lest! Fahrt! This is different from du (Nimm! Iss!).
cards.more: Imagine ihr as the calm sibling of du. When du gets excited, it changes its vowel: Nimm! Iss! Lies! The ihr form never does that. It keeps the stem of the infinitive and adds -t: nehm-t, ess-t, les-t, fahr-t. So the ihr command is always the infinitive without -en, plus -t. Step 1: take the infinitive: nehmen. Step 2: cut -en: nehm. Step 3: add -t: Nehmt! Extra example: Schlaft gut! = Sleep well (to two friends).
cards.lead: You can make ihr commands. Next: stem-changing verbs in the ihr command, which do not change, so you can say Take or Eat to a group.

deeper.text: Watch the spelling of two forms. essen gives ess + t = Esst, with a double s. lesen gives les + t = Lest, with one s. You hear almost the same sound, so check the infinitive when you write. Spoken quickly, Esst! and Lest! both sound short and sharp, which suits a command.

cards.title: sein and the extra e: Seid! Wartet!
cards.body: sein: ihr seid → Seid! Learn it: Seid bitte ruhig! Verbs with a stem ending in -t already have an e in the ihr form: ihr wartet → Wartet! ihr arbeitet → Arbeitet! No extra step is needed.
cards.more: Seid is the ihr form of sein you learned in chapter 2: ihr seid. The command looks the same, with the verb first. For warten and arbeiten, the e is already in the ihr form: ihr wartet. Step 1: ihr form. Step 2: remove ihr. Step 3: put the verb first. Extra example: Arbeitet nicht! = Do not work (to several people).
cards.lead: You know the ihr command shape. Next: sein and verbs with a t at the end of the stem, so you can say Be quiet or Wait to a group.

deeper.text: Seid (be!) and seit (since) sound exactly the same, but they are two different words. Seid with d is the ihr form of sein: Seid ruhig! seit with t means since: seit gestern. Only the spelling tells them apart, so check the meaning when you write. One sentence can even have both.

example.de: Seid ruhig, ich habe seit gestern Kopfschmerzen.
example.en: Be quiet, I have had a headache since yesterday.

cards.title: Separable verbs with ihr: Ruft an!
cards.body: Separable verbs split as always: the verb goes first, the prefix goes last. anrufen → Ruft an! aufstehen → Steht auf! mitkommen → Kommt mit! There is no ihr in the sentence.
cards.more: Picture a sports coach shouting to the team: Steht auf! Passt auf! Kommt mit! Every command is a sandwich: the verb on top, the prefix at the bottom. With ihr there is no Sie and no ihr in between, only the other words. When a ball flies towards someone, the coach shouts Vorsicht! Step 1: split the verb: auf + stehen. Step 2: the ihr form without ihr: Steht. Step 3: the prefix last. Extra example: Nehmt die Tasche mit! = Take the bag along.
cards.lead: You can make ihr commands with ordinary verbs. Next: separable verbs in the ihr command, so you can say Call me or Get up to a group.

deeper.text: The same frame again: verb first, prefix last. Passt auf! is what people say when you must be careful, and it is useful in real life. Aufpassen means to pay attention or to watch out. You will hear it from teachers, parents and friends, usually with a raised voice.

cards.title: Three commands side by side
cards.body: You now know all three. Sie: the infinitive + Sie. du: the stem (with e → i). ihr: the ihr form without ihr. sein: Seien Sie! Sei! Seid! Always check first who you are talking to.
steps: Sie (polite): Nehmen Sie eine Tablette!
du (one friend): Nimm eine Tablette!
ihr (friends): Nehmt eine Tablette!
cards.more: Think of three little doors. The first door is Sie: polite, with Sie at the back. The second is du: one friend, short, with the stem. The third is ihr: many friends, ending in -t. Step 1: who are you talking to? Step 2: open the right door. Step 3: put the verb first. The prefix always goes last. Extra example: Rufen Sie an! Ruf an! Ruft an! = Call! (three ways).
cards.lead: You now know three command forms. Next: Sie, du and ihr side by side, so you can see the three in one look and tell them apart.

deeper.text: When you speak to a person by name, put the name first and a comma after it: Mira, ruf bitte Ben an. The name is not part of the command, it only gets the person's attention. The verb stays the first word of the command itself.

cards.title: Who are you talking to? Tips for a group
cards.body: Pick the form by the person. A doctor to Herr Ali: Sie. Mira to Ben: du. Ben to Mira and Leon: ihr. In class, a teacher uses Sie for strangers and du or ihr for friends and children. When in doubt, use Sie. A group (die Gruppe) of friends hears ihr.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie dreimal am Tag eine Tablette.
examples.en: Take a tablet three times a day.
examples.why: The doctor to Herr Ali: Sie.

steps: One person you do not know well: Sie.
One friend: du.
Two or more friends: ihr.
cards.more: It is like choosing the right key. Step 1: count the people. One or more? Step 2: how well do you know them? Stranger or friend? Step 3: stranger: Sie. One friend: du. Several friends: ihr. If you are unsure, take Sie. Nobody is offended by a polite word. Extra example: Leon, sei ruhig! (du). Leon und Ben, seid ruhig! (ihr).
cards.lead: You can see all three forms together. Next: how to choose the right form for the person you speak to, so you pick the right command every time.

deeper.text: In many German offices, colleagues use du. Often the older or senior person offers it: Sag einfach du (just say du). Until someone offers, stay with Sie. Once you both say du, switch and stay with it. If you say du too early, it may sound rude, so being careful is the better choice at first.

example.de: Ich heiße Ben. Sag einfach du.
example.en: My name is Ben. Just say du.

cards.title: The sounds p/b, t/d, k/g
cards.body: p, t, k are hard, with a little puff of air: Pause, Tablette, Kopf. b, d, g are soft: Bett, Dienstag, gut. At the end of a word, b, d, g sound like p, t, k: Hand sounds like Hant, Tag sounds like Tak.

examples.why: B at the start is soft.
d at the end sounds like t: Hant.
g at the end sounds like k: Tak.

steps: Start of a word: p t k = hard, b d g = soft.
End of a word: b d g sound like p t k.
Say each word aloud, three times.
cards.more: Hold a hand in front of your mouth. Say Pause: you feel a puff of air. Say Bett: almost no puff. That is the whole difference at the start of a word. At the end of a word German is lazy: b, d and g all turn into their hard friends. So Tag ends in a k sound, Hand in a t sound. Step 1: say the pair Pause / Bett. Step 2: say Tag. Step 3: say Hand.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: the sounds p and b, t and d, k and g, so you can say words like Pause, Bett and Tag clearly.

deeper.text: There is an easy way to check: add an ending or look at the plural. Tag has a g, and it sounds like Tak. But the plural is Tage, and there you hear the g. Hand has a d, but Hände has a d you can hear. The spelling shows the soft letter when it is not at the end.

lessons.title: dürfen: what may I do?
lessons.goal: Ask for permission, say what is allowed or forbidden, and tell nicht dürfen from nicht müssen.

grammar.point: dürfen (darf, darfst, darf, dürfen, dürft, dürfen) is a modal verb: it is part 2 and the infinitive goes last; man is the general you; nicht dürfen = forbidden, nicht müssen = not necessary.
grammar.oneLine: Darf ich duschen? Hier darf man nicht rauchen. Du musst nicht arbeiten.

mistake.why: To say smoking is forbidden, use nicht dürfen. nicht müssen only says it is not necessary.

terms.meaning: may, to be allowed to
people in general, one: man darf
nicht dürfen = forbidden; nicht müssen = not necessary

cards.title: Before we start: what you may do
cards.body: At the doctor you ask: May I drink coffee? May I do sport? The verb dürfen asks for permission. It works like können, müssen and wollen from chapter 5, with the second verb at the end.
steps: You already know: Ich muss am Montag arbeiten: a modal verb (chapter 5)
New today: dürfen: darf is part 2, the other verb goes to the end; nicht dürfen means forbidden
By the end you can: ask for permission, say what is allowed or forbidden, and tell nicht dürfen from nicht müssen

examples.en: I have to work on Monday.
examples.why: You know this already. A modal verb in second place, the other verb last.
New today: dürfen asks for permission. The verb comes first in a question.
New today: man is the general you, and nicht dürfen means forbidden.

cards.more: Dürfen is another member of the modal family. You already know the family trick: the modal takes second place, the other verb waits at the end. What is new is the meaning. Dürfen is like a traffic light: you may, or you may not. Be careful with nicht müssen, which only means you do not have to. You will learn this step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: dürfen: all the forms
cards.body: dürfen means may or to be allowed to. It is a modal verb, like können and müssen: the modal is in part 2 and the other verb goes to the end. dürfen is irregular: ich darf, du darfst, er/sie darf, wir dürfen, ihr dürft, Sie dürfen.
cards.more: Dürfen works like können: ich kann, er kann (no ending) and ich darf, er darf. Step 1: learn the six forms. Step 2: the modal is in part 2. Step 3: the second verb is an infinitive, at the end. Notice the umlaut: darf (a) but dürfen (ü). Extra example: Anna darf Kaffee trinken. = Anna is allowed to drink coffee.
cards.lead: You know all the command forms. Next: dürfen, which means may or to be allowed to, so you can say what is permitted.

deeper.text: Look at the singular forms: ich darf and er darf are identical, with no ending. The same is true for kann and muss. That is a pattern for all modal verbs: ich and er, sie, es look the same. Then learn du darfst and ihr dürft. The wir, sie and Sie forms look like the infinitive.

cards.title: Ask for permission: Darf ich …?
cards.body: To ask if you may do something, start with the modal: Darf ich Kaffee trinken? It is a yes/no question: the verb is first, the second verb goes last. Yes: Ja, Sie dürfen. or Ja, bitte. No: Nein, das dürfen Sie nicht.

examples.why: A short no: das, dürfen, Sie, nicht.

steps: Ask: Darf ich … ?
Yes: Ja, Sie dürfen. / Ja, bitte.
No: Nein, das dürfen Sie nicht.
cards.more: Asking for permission is like knocking on a door. Step 1: knock with Darf ich? Step 2: say what you want, as an infinitive at the end: Darf ich duschen? Step 3: listen: Ja, bitte (yes) or Nein, das dürfen Sie nicht (no). In the short answer das means that, and the verb dürfen is in part 2. Extra example: Darf ich aufstehen? = May I get up?
cards.lead: You can say what is allowed. Next: asking for permission with Darf ich …?, so you can ask a doctor if you may drink or shower.

deeper.text: Darf ich is also a polite way to ask for something in daily life, not only at the doctor. It is a little more formal than Kann ich. In a café, at a meeting or on a train, Darf ich bitte …? sounds friendly and respectful. Native speakers use it all the time.

cards.title: man: you, one, people in general
cards.body: The little word man means people in general, like you or one in English. It uses the er/sie form of the verb: man darf. Rules on signs use man: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. It is not Mann (the male person).
cards.more: A sign cannot say you, because it talks to everyone. So German uses man. Step 1: man takes the same verb form as er: man darf. Step 2: a place can start the sentence: Hier darf man … Step 3: the infinitive goes last. Man with one n is the word on signs. Mann with two n's is a man. Extra example: Hier darf man essen. = You may eat here.
cards.lead: You can ask for permission. Next: the small word man, which means people in general, so you can read signs and rules.

deeper.text: man is also the best way to ask about a rule. Darf man hier rauchen? asks if smoking is allowed here, without asking about you personally. In a museum, a hospital or a train, this question is polite and very common. The answer often uses man too: Nein, hier darf man nicht rauchen.

cards.title: erlaubt or verboten?
cards.body: Two adjectives for rules: erlaubt (allowed) and verboten (forbidden). Use them with sein: Das ist erlaubt. Rauchen ist verboten. They say the same as dürfen: nicht dürfen = verboten. A sign (das Schild) often shows a rule (die Regel).
cards.more: At a German train station, many signs carry one of two words: erlaubt or verboten. Essen verboten. Rauchen verboten. They work like a green light and a red light. When you speak, you can use the same words with sein: Das ist verboten. Or you use dürfen: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. Step 1: read the rule. Step 2: say it with ist + erlaubt or verboten. Step 3: or say it with dürfen. Extra example: Telefonieren ist hier nicht erlaubt. = Phoning is not allowed here.
cards.lead: You know man for rules. Next: two words for allowed and forbidden, so you can say that something is allowed or that it is forbidden.

deeper.text: A verb used as a noun gets a capital letter: Rauchen ist verboten. The word means smoking, so it is written like a noun. On signs people often drop ist and just write Rauchen verboten. When you read a sign, look for the capital letter and for verboten or erlaubt.

cards.title: How long? Wie lange darf ich …?
cards.body: To ask how long a rule lasts, use Wie lange darf ich …? The answer is a time: drei Tage, eine Woche, bis Montag. You know Wie lange from chapter 5. Sie dürfen drei Tage nicht arbeiten. The two verbs: dürfen is part 2, the infinitive is last.

examples.de: Wie lange darf ich nicht arbeiten?
examples.en: How long may I not work?

examples.de: Sie dürfen drei Tage nicht arbeiten.
examples.en: You may not work for three days.

examples.de: Sie dürfen bis Montag nicht arbeiten.
examples.en: You may not work until Monday.

rows: Wie lange darf ich nicht arbeiten?
Wie lange darf ich nicht arbeiten?
Wie lange darf ich nicht arbeiten?

cards.more: Doctors always say how long. Step 1: ask Wie lange? Step 2: the answer is a length of time: drei Tage (three days), eine Woche (one week), or bis + a day. Step 3: nicht usually goes near the end, before the infinitive. The plural of Tag is Tage. Extra example: Sie dürfen eine Woche keinen Sport machen. = You may not do sport for a week.
cards.lead: You can say allowed and forbidden. Next: asking how long a rule lasts with Wie lange, so you can ask how many days you may not work.

deeper.text: A length of time needs no little word in German: drei Tage, eine Woche. English says for three days, but German says three days alone. The little word bis (until) gives an end point: bis Montag. So length has no word, and a date or day has bis.

example.de: Sie dürfen eine Woche nicht arbeiten.
example.en: You may not work for one week.

cards.title: nicht dürfen or nicht müssen?
cards.body: Careful! They do not mean the same. nicht dürfen = forbidden: Du darfst nicht arbeiten. (Stop!) nicht müssen = not necessary: Du musst nicht arbeiten. (You can, but you do not have to.) One small word changes the meaning.

examples.en: You do not have to work.

examples.de: Sie müssen nicht kommen, aber Sie dürfen kommen.
examples.en: You do not have to come, but you may.

cards.more: Think of a door. Nicht dürfen: the door is locked. You cannot go in. Nicht müssen: the door is open, but nobody forces you to go in. Step 1: forbidden? Say nicht dürfen. Step 2: only not necessary? Say nicht müssen. In English must not and do not have to confuse people too, but German keeps the meanings apart. Extra example: Ich muss nicht kommen. = I do not have to come.
cards.lead: You can ask how long a rule lasts. Next: the difference between nicht dürfen and nicht müssen, so you can tell forbidden apart from not necessary.

deeper.text: The same pair works with kein. Du darfst keinen Kaffee trinken means coffee is forbidden. Du musst keinen Kaffee trinken means nobody forces you, you can say no. People often use the second one to be kind, when it is your choice. So kein follows the same idea as nicht.

example.en: You do not have to take any tablets.

cards.title: At the doctor: may I? you may not
cards.body: At the doctor you ask Darf ich …? and the doctor answers with dürfen, or with nicht dürfen. The doctor can also use kein for things: Sie dürfen keinen Kaffee trinken. Masculine words take keinen, as in chapter 4.
steps: You: Darf ich duschen?
Doctor: Ja, Sie dürfen.
You: Darf ich baden?
Doctor: Nein, heute nicht.
You: Darf ich Kaffee trinken?
Doctor: Nein, Sie dürfen keinen Kaffee trinken.
cards.more: A visit to the doctor is full of may and may not. Step 1: ask your question with Darf ich? Step 2: the doctor says Ja or Nein. Step 3: for no, the doctor often uses keinen with a thing, or nicht with an action. A separable verb like aufstehen does not split after a modal: it goes to the end in one piece. Extra example: Darf ich aufstehen? = May I get up?
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: a short doctor dialogue about what you may and may not do, so you can ask Darf ich? and understand the answer.

deeper.text: kein follows the gender of the thing. After dürfen, a masculine thing takes keinen, a neuter thing takes kein, and a feminine or plural thing takes keine. So Sie dürfen kein Fleisch essen, but Sie dürfen keinen Kaffee trinken. Fleisch is neuter, and Kaffee is masculine.

The du form: the a-stem + -st.
The wir form looks like the infinitive.
The modal is first; trinken is last.

lessons.title: sollen: pass on an instruction
lessons.goal: Pass on what the doctor says with sollen and ask what you should do.

grammar.point: sollen (soll, sollst, soll, sollen, sollt, sollen) says someone told you to: it is part 2 and the infinitive goes last. Turn a command into Ich soll … and tell sollen, müssen and dürfen apart.
grammar.oneLine: Der Arzt sagt: Ich soll viel trinken. Was soll ich tun?

mistake.why: After a modal the second verb is an infinitive and goes to the end.

terms.meaning: to be supposed to: someone else said so
to tell someone else what was said
viel, wenig, zu viel

cards.title: Before we start: passing on an instruction
cards.body: The doctor says: Drink a lot. Later your friend asks what the doctor said. You report: I am supposed to drink a lot. The verb sollen does this job, with the same bracket as dürfen and müssen.
steps: You already know: Ich darf Sport machen with dürfen (last lesson), and commands (lessons 4 to 6)
New today: sollen says someone told you to: soll is part 2, the other verb goes to the end
By the end you can: pass on an instruction and tell sollen, müssen and dürfen apart

examples.why: You know this already. A modal verb with a second verb at the end.

examples.en: I am supposed to drink a lot.
examples.why: New today: sollen means someone told me to.

examples.de: Der Arzt sagt: Mira soll viel trinken.
examples.en: The doctor says: Mira is supposed to drink a lot.
examples.why: New today: sollen also passes on an instruction for someone else.

cards.more: A command is spoken to you. Sollen is how you carry that command to someone else, like a postman carrying a letter. The doctor says: Trink viel! You tell your friend: Ich soll viel trinken. The shape is the same as with the other modals: soll in second place, the other verb at the end. You will learn this step by step in the next cards, and you will also practise choosing between sollen, müssen and dürfen.

cards.title: sollen: someone told me to
cards.body: sollen means to be supposed to: someone else said so. Forms: ich soll, du sollst, er/sie soll, wir sollen, ihr sollt, Sie sollen. It works like können and wollen: the modal is part 2, the infinitive goes last. No umlaut here.

examples.en: I am supposed to drink a lot.
You are supposed to stay in bed.
We are supposed to take tablets.

cards.more: Sollen is a messenger verb. It means somebody else said so: the doctor, the teacher, your mother. Step 1: learn six forms, like wollen. Step 2: the modal is in part 2. Step 3: the other verb is an infinitive, at the end. Careful: ich soll and er soll have no ending. Extra example: Leon soll viel schlafen. = Leon is supposed to sleep a lot.
cards.lead: You can say what is allowed and not allowed. Next: sollen, which means supposed to, so you can say what someone told you to do.

deeper.text: Careful: sollen does not make the future. English shall can talk about tomorrow, but German simply uses the present with a time word: Morgen gehe ich zum Arzt. Ich soll morgen zum Arzt gehen means the doctor or someone else wants it. So soll always has a person behind it who gave the instruction.

example.en: Tomorrow I am going to the doctor.

cards.title: Pass on an instruction
cards.body: The doctor gives a command: Trinken Sie viel! You pass it on with sollen: Ich soll viel trinken. The command verb becomes the infinitive at the end, Sie disappears, and the modal takes the second place.

examples.en: I am supposed to drink a lot of water.
I am supposed to stay in bed.

examples.de: Ich soll dreimal am Tag eine Tablette nehmen.
examples.en: I am supposed to take a tablet three times a day.

steps: Doctor: Nehmen Sie eine Tablette!
You: Ich soll eine Tablette nehmen.
The verb goes to the end. Sie becomes ich.
cards.more: Passing on a message is like turning a command into a report. Step 1: write the command: Nehmen Sie eine Tablette! Step 2: put Ich soll in front. Step 3: the command verb moves to the end as an infinitive. Step 4: drop Sie. A separable verb stays in one piece: Rufen Sie an! becomes Ich soll anrufen. Extra example: Schlafen Sie viel! → Ich soll viel schlafen.
cards.lead: You know sollen for what someone told you. Next: turning a doctor's command into a sentence about yourself, so you can repeat the advice.

deeper.text: When you pass an instruction on, the possessive changes with the speaker. The doctor says Nehmen Sie Ihre Tablette. You say Ich soll meine Tablette nehmen. Ihr (your) becomes mein (my), because now you are the speaker. The command verb goes to the end as an infinitive.

example.en: I am supposed to take my tablets.

cards.title: Pass it on to someone else
cards.body: You can also tell a third person what to do: Leon soll im Bett bleiben. Often you say who gave the order: Der Arzt sagt: Leon soll im Bett bleiben. Use soll for one person, sollen for two or more. Separable verbs stay together: Ben soll anrufen.

examples.en: Leon is supposed to stay in bed.

examples.de: Der Arzt sagt: Mira soll viel trinken.
examples.en: The doctor says: Mira is supposed to drink a lot.
examples.why: sagen, then a colon, then a new sentence.

examples.en: Ben and Anna are supposed to call.

cards.more: Picture yourself as a messenger between the doctor and a friend's family. The doctor tells you, and you tell them: Leon soll im Bett bleiben. A name works like er or sie, so it takes soll. Two names take sollen. Often you start with Der Arzt sagt and a colon, so everyone knows who gave the order. Step 1: who must do it? Step 2: soll or sollen. Step 3: the infinitive last. Extra example: Frau Weber sagt: Ben soll früh aufstehen. = Frau Weber says: Ben is supposed to get up early.
cards.lead: You can pass on an instruction to yourself. Next: telling another person what to do with sollen, so you can say what someone else must do.

deeper.text: A separable verb stays whole after a modal. You say Ben soll anrufen, not Ben soll ruft an. The verb is at the end in one piece, and only the modal changes. This is the same rule you know from können and müssen in chapter 5.

example.en: Frau Weber is supposed to call.

cards.title: Soll ich …? What should I do?
cards.body: To ask what you are supposed to do, use sollen in a question. Soll ich zum Arzt gehen? Was soll ich tun? Wie oft soll ich die Tabletten nehmen? Wie lange soll ich im Bett bleiben? tun means to do.

examples.en: How often should I take the tablets?

steps: Ask: Was soll ich tun?
Doctor: Sie sollen im Bett bleiben.
Ask: Wie lange? Doctor: Eine Woche.
cards.more: Soll ich? is the question for orders and advice. It is like saying: what is the plan for me? Step 1: choose your question word: was, wie oft, wie lange. Step 2: soll in part 2. Step 3: ich. Step 4: the infinitive last. For a yes/no question start with Soll. The verb tun means to do. You know tut weh from lesson 1: it is a form of tun. Extra example: Soll ich anrufen? = Should I call?
cards.lead: You can say what someone should do. Next: asking what you should do with Soll ich …?, so you can ask the doctor for advice.

deeper.text: Soll ich …? is also how you offer help. It means shall I? and is a friendly question: Soll ich die Tür aufmachen? The other person can answer Ja, bitte or Nein, danke. English uses shall I here too, so the idea is the same.

cards.title: sollen, müssen or dürfen?
cards.body: Three modals, three ideas. Ich soll: someone told me. Ich muss: it is necessary. Ich darf: it is allowed. The grammar is the same for all of them: modal in part 2, infinitive last. Only the idea changes. Pick the one that fits.

examples.en: I am supposed to take tablets.
I must go to the doctor.

cards.more: Ask yourself one question: where does the rule come from? Step 1: from another person: sollen. Step 2: from the situation, you have no choice: müssen. Step 3: from permission, you are free: dürfen. All three sit in part 2 and push the infinitive to the end. Extra example: Ich soll viel schlafen. Ich muss früh aufstehen. Ich darf Sport machen.
cards.lead: You can ask what you should do. Next: comparing sollen, müssen and dürfen, so you can pick the modal verb that fits the idea you want.

deeper.text: müssen is stronger than sollen. Ich muss means there is no choice, a fact or a duty. Ich soll means someone asked me to. You might ignore a soll, but a muss is a must. In a doctor's office both appear, so listen for which one the doctor uses.

example.en: I have to get up early today.

cards.title: How much, how often: viel, wenig, regelmäßig
cards.body: Doctors talk about amounts. viel = a lot. wenig = little. zu viel = too much. They come after the verb: Ich soll viel trinken. Ich soll nicht zu viel arbeiten. For no, use nicht, or kein for a thing: Du sollst keinen Kaffee trinken.

steps: Do it a lot: viel.
Do it a little: wenig.
Do not do it too much: nicht zu viel.
cards.more: Amounts are small words that sit in the middle of the sentence. Step 1: viel is the plus word. Step 2: wenig is the minus word. Step 3: zu viel is the too-much word, and nicht zu viel says not too much. Step 4: for a thing you may not have, use keinen, keine or kein. Extra example: Ich soll wenig Fleisch essen. = I am supposed to eat little meat.
cards.lead: You can choose between three modal verbs. Next: words for amounts, viel, wenig and zu viel, so you can say how much to do or drink.

deeper.text: viel and wenig stand before a thing and have no ending with words like Tee or Kaffee. Say viel Tee, wenig Kaffee, with no article. You use them just like English a lot of and a little. Doctors use both words very often when they talk about food and drink.

example.en: You are supposed to drink little coffee.

cards.body: At the end of a visit, the doctor gives several commands. You pass them on, for example to Mira. Use ich soll for yourself and du sollst when someone tells you. Mix viel, wenig, nicht, bis and zweimal am Tag. It is all about die Gesundheit (health); die Medizin (medicine) is one part.

Step 4: keep the time and amount words in the middle. Your friend says Gute Besserung! Extra example: Der Arzt sagt: Ich soll dreimal am Tag Tropfen nehmen.
cards.lead: Last card of this lesson: all the doctor's advice together, so you can pass on several instructions in one talk, to yourself or to someone else.

deeper.text: die Gesundheit means health, and Gesundheit! is also what Germans say when someone sneezes, like bless you. The answer is Danke! Do not mix it up with Gute Besserung!, which you say to someone who is ill. One is for a sneeze, the other is for an illness that lasts some days.
